scenario: AITA for calling out my lying coworker? | So i work with this tub of lard named jackson, all the time he constantly talks shit about how good he is at fighting and how he could kick anyones ass and how "before i got out of my prime and flabby i was a 23-0 pro boxer, one of the best in the valley". Now i know for a fact this is all bullshit, if he really went 23-0 as a pro boxer surely something would show up when i google his name right. Anyway im 19 and have been training muay thai for 8 years (still am), and wrestled in high school, i am very fit and am very proud of my progress in martial arts and fitness considering i too was once a tub of lard. I rarely hang out with him outside of work becuase he never shuts up about this shit, and other lies including "i could have graduated cullinary school with high honors but i got kicked out for fighting" and "i know high profile gangbangers who make millions a year, thats why i work in this resturant, for fun, not becuase i need too". The majority of them think im an asshole, although a few agree with me. For background info hes 29, im 19. And it was just the two of us when i called him out but i will admit i told some of the coworkers i liked.

message.reasoning:
Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether the action in this scenario is morally acceptable or not. Let me read through the scenario again to make sure I understand it properly.

So, there's this person who works with someone named Jackson. Jackson is described as a "tub of lard," which is a bit derogatory, but I guess it's just a description. Jackson constantly brags about his fighting skills, claiming he was a 23-0 pro boxer and one of the best in the valley. The person knows this is probably not true because if he were that good, there should be some record of it online. 

The person in question is 19, has been training in muay thai for eight years, and was also a wrestler in high school. They're fit and proud of their progress, especially since they used to be overweight too. They don't hang out with Jackson much outside of work because he's always lying about his achievements, like getting kicked out of culinary school for fighting and knowing high-profile gangbangers who make millions. 

One day, they were hanging out, having beers, and watching UFC. Jackson made a comment about being able to KO the fighters in the match, and the person snapped, calling him out on his lies. They told Jackson they doubted he could even kick their ass, even though they're half his weight and only 19. They also challenged him to come to their muay thai gym, saying they'd maul him. Jackson got upset and left, and the person told their coworkers about it. Most coworkers think the person is an asshole, but a few agree with them. Jackson is 29, and the person is 19. It was just the two of them when the person called him out, but they did tell some coworkers about it.

So, the question is: Is it morally acceptable for the person to call out Jackson on his lies? The options are to answer 1 if it's acceptable and 0 if it's not, along with an excuse.

First, I need to consider the context. The person is younger, 19, and has legitimate credentials in martial arts. Jackson is 29 and seems to be exaggerating his skills and past. The person is frustrated with Jackson's constant lying and decides to confront him publicly, which leads to Jackson leaving and the person spreading the incident among coworkers.

Now, is calling someone out on their lies morally acceptable? Generally, honesty is valued, but the way it's done matters. Confronting someone in public, especially in a setting where others are present, can be seen as embarrassing or hurtful, even if the intent is to expose the truth.

In this case, the person was drinking, which might have lowered their inhibitions, leading to the confrontation. Also, by telling coworkers about it, they're potentially spreading gossip and could be contributing to a negative work environment.

On the other hand, the person is standing up for themselves and others who might be misled by Jackson's lies. They're asserting their own skills and challenging the false claims. However, the method of confrontation and the subsequent spreading of the incident could be seen as unprofessional and mean-spirited.

I think the key points are:
1. The person's intent was to expose the truth about Jackson's lies.
2. The method of confrontation was public and possibly hurtful.
3. The person then shared the incident with coworkers, which could be seen as gossiping.

Considering these points, while the intent might be justified, the method and aftermath could be seen as morally unacceptable because they involve public embarrassment and spreading the incident, which could harm workplace relationships.
